Fugue in G Minor, BWV 578

J. S. Bach’s organ fugue, analyzed with Scott Roberts’s six-step method (2004). Roberts reads the whole fugue as one idea worked out at every level: expansion. The subject widens its intervals, its period is lopsided (2 + 2½ bars), and the episodes between entries keep getting longer. Every label on the score below comes from his tables and figures; what this page adds is listed under About This Score.

  • 68 bars, 4/4
  • 4 voices: two manuals and pedal
  • 9 integrants (entries)
  • 5 digressions, 2 → 8½ bars
  • No stretto, inversion, augmentation or diminution

The Six Steps

Roberts’s method in order. Each card gives his rule Roberts and what it finds in BWV 578. The buttons set up the score for that step.

  1. STEP 1

    Identify the Traditional Fugue Elements

    Mark every subject and answer entry, the countersubject, codettas, episodes and coda, each with its voice and key, plus any devices such as stretto or augmentation.

    • Nine entries: soprano, alto, tenor, bass, tenor → soprano, alto, bass, soprano, bass.
    • Keys g, d, g, d, g → B♭, B♭, B♭, c, g.
    • A countersubject from m. 6 that comes back in every later entry except the first. It often moves from voice to voice mid-entry (Roberts’s “transfers”).
    • No subject devices at all, so Roberts leaves that row out of his table.
  2. STEP 2

    Find the Notable Properties of the Exposition

    Look for anything unusual or distinctive: linear ascents or descents (complete or “blocked”), rhythmic and melodic patterns, a “suspended” scale degree, contrasting material, and structural units.

    • A period: a 2-bar phrase ending on a half cadence, then a 2½-bar phrase ending on an authentic cadence. The halves are unequal.
    • Contrast: an active first phrase, then a static one that circles 1̂–2̂–3̂ over a held dominant.
    • Descending arpeggio D–B♭–G, mm. 1–2.
    • The opening perfect fifth as bookends: rising G–D to start, falling A–D to close the first phrase.
    • Expansion: in the second phrase a falling fourth widens to a fifth, then a sixth.
  3. STEP 3

    Look for Patterns in the Structure

    Call the entries integrants and the episodes digressions. Look for sections that get steadily longer or shorter, lengths that mirror each other, and length ratios such as 1:2 or 3:2.

    • The digressions grow: A 2, B 3, C 3½, D 5, E 8½ bars.
    • D = A + B and E = C + D.
    • C’s 3½ bars equal the 3½ bars added to period V, the only integrant longer than 4½ bars.
  4. STEPS 4–5

    Segment by Significant Phenomena; Repeat Step 3 Not applicable

    Step 4 cuts the fugue a second way when the entry-and-episode plan is incoherent, or the rhythm, texture or density changes sharply, or entries group into larger blocks. Step 5 reruns step 3 on that new plan.

    Roberts finds none of these in BWV 578, so both steps are skipped. The traditional plan already carries the pattern.

  5. STEP 6

    Decide How the Fugue Responds

    If the music later “reconciles” its notable properties (brings them back with the trait that made them notable, worked out), the approach is rhetorical. If not, it is literal.

    Rhetorical. The expansion in the subject returns as the structure: ever-longer digressions, a broadened central period V, and digressions built from the subject’s own intervals. The final bass fifth D–G answers the opening fifth G–D.

Growing Digressions

Step 3 in one picture. Each digression is longer than the one before, and the lengths add up like a running sum.

  • D (5) = A (2) + B (3)
    the first two digressions together
  • E (8½) = C (3½) + D (5)
    the next two together
  • C (3½) = period V’s added bars
    1 bar of interpolation + 2½ bars of cadential extension

Roberts pairs this with the subject itself: the digressions are the active, changing part of the fugue, like the subject’s first phrase, and the integrants are the static, repeated part, like its second.

A Rhetorical Fugue

What the Integrants Do Roberts

Every integrant is a period built from the same two lines, subject and countersubject, plus a pedal point or a filler voice. Four of the nine put the subject in the bass and the countersubject on top. Played back to back without the digressions they would sound redundant, and the last entry (IX) repeats the third (III) in key and content.

What the Digressions Do Roberts

So the digressions carry the argument. They grow in length, and they draw their material from the subject’s notable properties: A turns the arpeggio and the falling fourth upside down; B joins the rising fourth to the subject’s falling third; C widens the fourth to a sixth; D combines them over a full circle of fifths, with the only pedal part in any digression; E gathers all of them, breaks the circle at G minor, and climbs in rising fourths to the final entry.

The Rhetorical Reading Roberts

Roberts reads the first integrant as a thesis and each digression as an argument for it. Each return of the thesis is heard as more convincing, until nothing is left to argue and the fugue ends. Without stretto, inversion or augmentation to vary the subject, the lengthening digressions are what keep the repeats fresh.

The cadence at m. 58 is the same one that closes the fugue. Ending there would have been an anticlimax after a run of falling figures, so the music rises instead to a triumphant last entry, whose final bass fifth D–G resolves the opening rising fifth.

Roberts himself calls these narrative statements speculative and interpretive, but grounded in the analysis, and sets them apart from fanciful program notes (his footnote 16).

About This Score

Notes and Layout

The notes were taken from Pierre Gouin’s MIDI realization (CC BY-SA 4.0) and checked bar by bar against the Bach-Gesellschaft edition (BG 38, pp. 116–120). Where they differ, the score follows BG: trills appear as signs, not realized notes, voices follow the printed stems and staves, and a few pitches were corrected (for example m. 14 beat 3, m. 63 beat 1). Line breaks follow the BG print. Roberts quotes the Neue Bach-Ausgabe (IV/6); bar numbers agree.

Playback realizes the trills, starting on the upper note, and the pralltriller in m. 1. It uses recorded samples: the Steinway Grand by default, a harpsichord at A = 415, or a pipe organ with separate pedal pipes at A = 465. That is Chorton, the high “choir pitch” of the north and central German organs Bach played (harpsichords and other chamber instruments used the lower Kammerton). The organ samples are a modern church organ’s principal stop, not a restored baroque instrument: the closest freely licensed recording available.

What Is Roberts and What Is Ours

  • Roberts Section boundaries, lengths and keys (Tables 4–6), the entry, cadence and transfer labels (Figure 13), period V (Figure 14), the digression properties and chord rows (Figure 15), and the step 6 reading.
  • ours Which notes belong to the subject or countersubject (template matching, checked against his labels); where a cadence label sits within its bar (the dominant arrival for HC, the downbeat of the next phrase for IAC and PAC, as his period lengths imply); and the bracket placement of the notable properties.
